qualityGates.detail: Actual copy, prices and imagery — or content clearly marked as sample with DemoContentBadge.
One dominant action per page, and the module visibly supports it.
Checked at 320px, not assumed from a desktop breakpoint. No sideways scrolling.
Reachable and operable with Tab, arrows, Enter and Escape. Focus is always visible.
Every animation has a prefers-reduced-motion branch that keeps the content.
Nothing found, nothing saved, request failed — each has its own designed screen.

meta.closingNote: A practical rule: build every module with real content, a conversion purpose, a mobile layout, keyboard support, reduced-motion behavior, and an empty/error state before adding any visual “elite” layer. That is what makes the system hard to replicate: not one dramatic homepage, but a complete, coherent library of business-grade components.

sections.title: Global system modules
sections.blurb: These appear across nearly every site.

sections.title: Hero and attention modules
sections.blurb: Use one hero pattern per page, not five competing effects.

sections.title: Value and explanation modules
sections.blurb: These explain what the business does and why it matters.

sections.title: Proof and trust modules
sections.blurb: Proof should match the claim: metrics for performance claims, named testimonials for service claims, certifications for compliance claims.

sections.title: Conversion modules
sections.blurb: Every template needs one dominant conversion path; secondary actions should support, not compete with it.

sections.title: Commerce modules
sections.blurb: Catalogue, basket and checkout — the parts that must never be wrong about price or stock.

sections.title: Booking, scheduling, and operations
sections.blurb: Booking is a calendar problem before it is a design problem.

sections.title: Location and local SEO modules
sections.blurb: Local businesses should show consistent name, address, phone, hours, map, and booking/contact paths.

sections.title: Content and SEO modules
sections.blurb: Content modules carry most of the search weight; structure decides whether they get read.

sections.title: People, team, and culture
sections.blurb: People pages convert service businesses; they need credentials, not portraits alone.

sections.title: Hospitality and food modules
sections.blurb: Menus, rooms and reservations change weekly — model them so an operator can update without a developer.

sections.title: Real estate and property modules
sections.blurb: Listings live or die on filter fidelity, map sync and how fast a photo grid loads.

sections.title: Automotive modules
sections.blurb: Vehicle stock changes hourly; the site must reflect that or it becomes a brochure.

sections.title: Education and learning modules
sections.blurb: Learners need to see the path, the commitment and the proof before they enrol.

sections.title: Events, venues, and entertainment
sections.blurb: Events are date-bound, capacity-bound and timezone-bound — all three must be modelled.

sections.title: B2B, SaaS, and enterprise modules
sections.blurb: Strong SaaS architecture usually centers on product, solutions/use cases, pricing, resources, about, contact, demo, and login.

sections.title: Finance, legal, and regulated modules
sections.blurb: In regulated sectors the design job is disclosure: earn trust without overpromising in writing.

sections.title: Nonprofit and public-sector modules
sections.blurb: Mission, impact and money must be equally legible — donors and auditors read the same site.

sections.title: Motion, interaction, and premium layers
sections.blurb: Use these only after the functional site is excellent. Motion should support hierarchy rather than obscure content.

sections.title: Forms, validation, and feedback
sections.blurb: Every form needs labels, inline validation, accessible errors, success confirmation, and a privacy/consent explanation.
